claims.evidence: This is an observation from the literature with an inferred consequence, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Larger TCR cluster size increases the probability of T cell activation.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, larger TCR cluster size increases the probability of T cell activation (Manz et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Shorter binding events that overlapped in space and time activated NFAT translocation similar to long-lived single binding events in primary murine T cells.
claims.source: Lin et al., 2019, also observed cooperativity between single TCR/pMHC-binding events, where shorter binding events that overlapped in space and time activated NFAT translocation similar to long-lived single binding events in primary murine T cells.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Timothy McKeithan postulated that a kinetic proofreading system with slower reset rates for downstream events would respond to cognate-antigen more frequently while still ignoring weak self-antigen.
claims.source: Work on kinetic proofreading often assumes that the reset rate after ligand binding is uniform across all signaling intermediates (koff, Figure 1A). However, in his seminal work applying the mathematical framework of kinetic proofreading to TCR activation, Timothy McKeithan postulated that a kinetic proofreading system with slower reset rates for downstream events compared to upstream signaling events would respond to true cognate-antigen-binding events a higher percentage of the time while still ignoring weak self-antigen-binding events (McKeithan, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Harris et al. quantified the reset rate of Ca++ release to be 29 seconds and ERK phosphorylation to be 3 minutes upon signal inhibition.
claims.source: Recently, Harris et al. quantified the reset rate of the downstream signaling events Ca++ release and ERK phosphorylation upon signal inhibition to be 29 s and 3 min, respectively (Harris et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Both Ca++ and ERK levels can persist across short inhibitions of signaling.
claims.source: They showed both Ca++ and ERK levels can persist across short inhibitions of signaling.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from Harris et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The dissolution of LAT clusters is directly triggered by the unbinding of ligand from the TCR.
claims.source: The dissolution of LAT clusters is directly triggered by the unbinding of ligand from the TCR, and both the TCR and LAT are de-phosphorylated by CD45.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations in this study.

claims.claim: The rate of ERK dephosphorylation or cytosolic Ca++ depletion is not accelerated by TCR unbinding.
claims.source: To our knowledge, the rate of ERK dephosphorylation or cytosolic Ca++ depletion is not accelerated by TCR unbinding, and is turned over through constant rather than agonist-gated degradation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Cooperativity between active receptors could explain T cell activation in response to intermediate affinity self- and tumor antigens.
claims.source: Cooperativity between active receptors to complete downstream proofreading steps could explain observations of T cell activation in response to intermediate affinity self- and tumor antigens (Yin et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observations in the literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cooperativity mechanisms have been implicated in autoimmunity.
claims.source: Such a cooperativity mechanism has been implicated in autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) and immunotherapy off-target effects (Cameron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claims.claim: Cooperativity mechanisms have been implicated in immunotherapy off-target effects.
claims.source: Such a cooperativity mechanism has been implicated in autoimmunity (Korem Kohanim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) and immunotherapy off-target effects (Cameron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claims.claim: Jurkats on ICAM-1 functionalized bilayers released a greater percentage of bound LOV2 ligand upon blue-light illumination compared to antibody-based adhesion.
claims.source: Compared to our previous antibody-based adhesion, Jurkats on ICAM-1 functionalized bilayers released a greater percentage of the bound LOV2 ligand upon blue-light illumination.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two adhesion methods.

claims.claim: ICAM-1 adhered cells displayed receptor/Zap70 and LAT clustering spatial patterns similar to those observed with native receptor ligands on SLBs.
claims.source: ICAM-1 adhered cells also displayed receptor/Zap70 and LAT clustering spatial patterns similar to those observed by others using native receptor ligands on SLBs (Balagopalan et al., 2015; Chakraborty and Weiss, 2014; Kumari et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the current study compared to literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The lentiviral vectors used result in cell-to-cell variability in expression levels of constructs.
claims.source: The lentiviral vectors we used to express our zdk-CAR and live-cell biosensors result in cell-to-cell variability in the expression level of each construct, even after sorting for cells with CAR expression levels similar to native TCR expression in T cells (Tischer and Weiner, 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the experimental system.

claims.claim: Native T cells vary in TCR expression level and can respond to antigen even at very low levels of TCR expression.
claims.source: Importantly, the variability in receptor expression is not unique to our CAR system; native T cells also vary in TCR expression level and can respond to antigen even at very low levels of TCR expression (Labrecque et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a known property of native T cells, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Kinetic proofreading systems behave differently than non-proofreading systems at steady state.
claims.source: Kinetic proofreading systems behave differently than non-proofreading systems at steady state.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical property of kinetic proofreading systems.

claims.claim: A non-proofreading system's steady-state output is set by the number of ligand-bound receptors and not the binding half-lives of those ligands.
claims.source: A non-proofreading system's steady-state output is set by the number of ligand-bound receptors and not the binding half-lives of those ligands (Figure 3D, left; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical property demonstrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: A kinetic proofreading system can produce different steady-state outputs in response to ligands of different binding half-lives, even when ligand densities are adjusted to achieve equivalent occupancy.
claims.source: In contrast, a kinetic proofreading system can produce different steady-state outputs in response to ligands of different binding half-lives, even when ligand densities are adjusted to achieve equivalent occupancy (Daniels et al., 2006; Figure 3D, right; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical property demonstrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, with citation support.

claims.claim: Signaling events take varying amounts of time to occur after ligand binding on the order of tens of seconds.
claims.source: Signaling events take varying amounts of time to occur after ligand binding (Lin et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2019). However, the temporal delays between steps are on the order of tens of seconds.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claims.claim: Models with unique N values for all three signaling steps (Zap70, LAT, DAG) have the lowest AIC and best explain the data.
claims.source: Models with unique N values for all three signaling steps have the lowest AIC, thus best explaining our data.
claims.evidence: This is a result from AIC model selection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Models where LAT and DAG share the same N value have only marginally worse AIC than models with unique N values.
claims.source: However, models where LAT and DAG share the same N value (and Zap70 has a unique N value) have only marginally worse AIC (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is a result from AIC model selection analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: An 11-step kinetic proofreading system could achieve an error rate less than 0.001 at moderate half-life ratios and concentration ratios.
claims.source: At moderate half-life ratios, an 11-step network can discriminate cognate peptides present in small concentrations (e.g. 1 cognate-ligand per 1000 self-ligands at a half-life ratio of 6).
claims.evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: An 11-step network is insufficient to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, even at equal concentrations of cognate- and self-ligand.
claims.source: However, an 11-step network is insufficient to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, even at the high ligand ratio of 1 (equal concentrations of cognate- and self-ligand).
claims.evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis.

claims.claim: Cells are likely detecting longer-lived binding events from the underlying distribution of half-lives rather than the average ligand-binding half-life.
claims.source: This suggests that our cells are unlikely to be detecting the average ligand-binding half-life of each blue-light condition, but are more likely detecting longer-lived binding events from the underlying distribution of half-lives.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental conditions.

claims.claim: In vitro washout measurements may differ from the half-lives of ligand-receptor interactions between the cell's plasma membrane and the supported lipid bilayer.
claims.source: Another possibility is that our in vitro washout measurements, which measure average ligand-binding half-lives of soluble ligands diffusing in three dimensions, differ from the half-lives of ligand-receptor interactions between the cell's plasma membrane and the supported lipid bilayer diffusing in two dimensions (Huang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy, with citation support.

claims.claim: At least 14 steps are needed to discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2 when ligands are at equal concentrations.
claims.source: To discriminate between ligands with a half-life ratio of 2, at least 14 steps are needed when the ligands are at equal concentrations, and more than 25 steps are needed if cognate-ligands are 1 per 1000 self-ligands.
claims.evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: The required number of proofreading steps decreases rapidly as the half-life ratio increases.
claims.source: The required number of proofreading steps decreases rapidly as the half-life ratio increases, reaching a minimum of eight steps needed for a concentration ratio of 1 per 1000 and a half-life ratio of 10, which is more in line with physiological half-life ratios between agonist and non-agonist peptides (Davis et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a result from modeling analysis with citation to physiological parameters.

claims.claim: The fit N values may be somewhat inflated due to using average ligand-binding half-lives from three-dimensional washout experiments instead of two-dimensional single-molecule information.
claims.source: After comparing our results with the Ganti model, this analysis suggests that our number of fit proofreading steps may be somewhat inflated as a function of our uses the average ligand-binding half-lives of three-dimensional washout experiments in place of the two-dimensional single-molecule information T cells use to make activation decisions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling analysis results.

claims.claim: The higher fit N values are more consistent with the required number of steps to discriminate ligands under physiological conditions than the previous measurements of approximately three steps.
claims.source: However, the higher fit N values are more consistent with the required number of steps to discriminate ligands under more physiological conditions than our previous measurements of approximately three steps, which would not be expected to discriminate ligands with half-life ratio of 10 even at a ligand ratio of 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, right).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation comparing current and previous results to theoretical predictions.

results.result: The study addresses a knowledge gap regarding the location of kinetic proofreading computation in T cell signaling. Previous work by the authors established that T cells use kinetic proofreading for antigen discrimination and found significant proofreading at DAG generation, but lacked the ability to determine where upstream proofreading steps originate.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C19-C20 establish the background and motivation for the study. These claims are well-supported by citations to prior literature (C1, C19) and the authors' previous work (C3, C4, C5). The knowledge gap (C2, C20) is clearly articulated and provides appropriate context for the current investigation.

results.result: The optogenetic system was improved by replacing antibody-based adhesion with ICAM-1 adhesion, which enhanced the spatiotemporal dynamics of LOV2 binding, Zap70 recruitment, LAT clustering, and DAG generation biosensors. ICAM-1 adhesion resulted in statistically significant improvements in maximum fold-change for all biosensors and produced spatial patterns similar to native receptor ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C25-C30, C69-C70 describe methodological improvements that are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 2. The statistical significance of improvements (C30) is demonstrated with p-values, and the comparison to native systems (C70) is supported by citations. This represents a critical technical advance enabling the main findings.

results.result: Zap70 recruitment exhibits moderate kinetic proofreading with n=4.5 ± 0.4 proofreading steps, correlating with both receptor occupancy (ρ=0.42) and ligand-binding half-life (ρ=0.49). This suggests the existence of kinetic proofreading steps between ligand binding and Zap70 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C39 are supported by quantitative model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 4A and correlation analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A. The finding of moderate proofreading at Zap70 recruitment represents a key advance over previous work where no proofreading was detected at this level, enabled by the improved ICAM-1 adhesion method.

results.result: LAT clustering shows stronger kinetic proofreading with n=7.8 ± 1.1 proofreading steps compared to Zap70 recruitment. LAT clustering showed increased dependency on binding half-life (ρ=0.54) and decreased dependence on receptor occupancy (ρ=0.21), suggesting additional kinetic proofreading steps exist between Zap70 recruitment and LAT cluster formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C38 are supported by quantitative model fitting shown in Figure 4B and correlation analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B. The progressive increase in proofreading strength from Zap70 to LAT provides evidence for distributed proofreading steps throughout the signaling cascade.

results.result: DAG generation shows the highest degree of kinetic proofreading with n=11.3 ± 1.5 proofreading steps. DAG generation depended heavily on ligand half-life (ρ=0.52) while depending least on occupancy (ρ=0.18).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by quantitative model fitting shown in Figure 4C and correlation analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C. The highest proofreading strength at DAG generation suggests additional proofreading steps beyond LAT clustering, consistent with the distributed proofreading model.

results.result: The strength of kinetic proofreading progressively increases from Zap70 recruitment (n=4.5) to LAT clustering (n=7.8) to DAG generation (n=11.3), suggesting proofreading steps exist throughout the cascade up to DAG generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C37 synthesize the findings from C31, C33, and C35. The progressive increase in n values is clearly demonstrated in Figure 4D across three biological replicates. This represents the central finding of the paper regarding distributed kinetic proofreading.

results.result: Reset kinetics differ between signaling events: LOV2 unbinding (3.3s) and Zap70 dissociation (9.3s) fit exponential distributions suggesting one-step reset processes, while LAT cluster dissociation (14.2s) fits a two-step Erlang distribution, indicating LAT clusters reset through a slower multistep process.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by lifetime distribution analysis shown in Figure 5C. The different distribution fits (exponential vs. Erlang) and progressively longer mean lifetimes provide quantitative evidence for differential reset rates. The statistical approach of fitting to Poisson-based distributions is appropriate for this type of data.

results.result: Downstream signaling events have slower reset rates than upstream events, suggesting a distributed kinetic proofreading mechanism with proofreading steps at both the receptor and slower-resetting downstream signaling complexes. LAT clusters could potentially survive momentary ligand unbinding events and integrate multiple binding events.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 are supported by the reset rate data (C40-C44), but C45 is explicitly speculative and awaits experimental verification. While the slower LAT reset rate is well-documented, the functional consequence of signal integration across multiple binding events remains hypothetical. The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty.

results.result: AIC model selection analysis indicates that models with unique N values for all three signaling steps (Zap70, LAT, DAG) best explain the data, though models where LAT and DAG share the same N value have only marginally worse AIC.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by AIC analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5. The use of AIC for model selection is appropriate for comparing nested models with different numbers of parameters. The marginal difference for LAT/DAG models is consistent with the flat residual landscapes noted in the text.

results.result: Modeling analysis using the Ganti framework suggests that an 11-step system can discriminate ligands at moderate half-life ratios but is insufficient at a ratio of 2. The fit N values may be somewhat inflated due to using average 3D washout measurements rather than 2D single-molecule information, but are more consistent with physiological discrimination requirements than previous measurements of ~3 steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C86 involve theoretical modeling and interpretation. While the Ganti model analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) is appropriately applied, the authors acknowledge significant uncertainty about whether cells detect average half-lives or longer-lived events from the distribution (C81), and potential discrepancies between 3D and 2D measurements (C82, C85). The interpretation is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: The Discussion integrates findings with existing literature on potential molecular mechanisms underlying kinetic proofreading, including CD45 exclusion, receptor conformational changes, Lck and Zap70 activation, LAT phosphorylation, spatial organization of signaling complexes, and potential cooperativity mechanisms relevant to autoimmunity and immunotherapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C68 represent integration of the current findings with established literature. These claims are appropriately supported by citations and represent reasonable interpretations of how the observed distributed proofreading could be mechanistically implemented. The speculative elements (C47, C66) are appropriately identified as such.

results.result: The experimental system exhibits cell-to-cell variability in construct expression due to lentiviral vectors, which is similar to native T cell TCR expression variability. Kinetic proofreading systems behave differently than non-proofreading systems at steady state, with proofreading systems producing different outputs for ligands with different half-lives even at equivalent occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 describe properties of the experimental system and theoretical foundations. C71-C72 acknowledge a limitation while noting biological relevance (supported by citation). C73-C75 describe fundamental properties of kinetic proofreading systems, demonstrated in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. These provide important context for interpreting the steady-state measurements.
